content.rendered:
It has become a familiar ritual and, of course, an annual nightmare of sorts across Nigerian cities. Dark clouds gather and the rain begins. What ought to bring relief in the form of cooler weather and fresh air instead sends anxiety through communities. Motorists scramble for higher ground, commuters abandon vehicles, businesses shut their doors, and social media fills with videos of submerged roads, stranded families and floating cars. Within hours, another “disaster” is trending. Yet the real tragedy is that none of it is surprising or new. It happens every year.

One would have expected that by now, governments at all levels would have learnt from previous experiences and taken proactive measures to minimise the annual ordeal. Sadly, each rainy season seems to catch both the authorities and many residents unprepared, despite the fact that the warning signs have become as predictable as the rains themselves.

Why should an ordinary act of nature become an annual national emergency? Rain is natural, while disasters are largely man-made. It is evident that some countries with far heavier rainfall do not grind to a halt simply because the heavens opened. Rain, in itself, rarely kills. The destruction is often caused by poor planning, blocked drainage systems, weak institutions and a culture of negligence. Rain is an act of God; disasters are often acts of human negligence.

The causes of Nigeria’s flooding problem are not far-fetched. They are glaring enough for all to see. They come in the form of poor urban planning, indiscriminate construction of buildings on flood plains, uncontrolled reclamation of wetlands and road construction without adequate drainage infrastructure. Examples abound in major cities and remote communities across the country. From Lagos to Port Harcourt, Ibadan to Benin, and even smaller towns, the same ugly pattern repeats itself every rainy season.

The irony is that most drainage systems, where they are available, do not drain in the real sense of the word. More often than not, they have been turned into refuse dumps, with waste deliberately thrown into gutters or washed into them by floodwaters after being indiscriminately discarded elsewhere. Some drainage channels have not been desilted for years, while construction debris and silt block many others. Consequently, water that ought to flow freely has nowhere to go except onto roads, into homes and business premises.

It is also common to see newly completed roads without adequate attention paid to drainage.

In some places, drains are either too narrow to cope with heavy rainfall or terminate abruptly without proper outlets. The result is predictable: roads become rivers within minutes of a heavy rainfall. Public infrastructure that should serve the people instead becomes part of the problem.

Building approvals also deserve a second look. Approvals are often granted, but enforcement is weak or completely absent. This has contributed significantly to the proliferation of illegal structures and buildings erected on waterways and floodplains. In many instances, political interference prevents the removal of such structures, while compromised enforcement agencies look the other way. The consequences are borne not only by those who erected the buildings but by entire communities whenever flooding occurs.

The effects of these reckless practices are worsened by climate change. Rising global temperatures have contributed to more intense rainfall, rising sea levels and increasingly extreme weather conditions. Climate experts have repeatedly warned that such weather events will become more frequent and severe. However, it is important to add that climate change exposes weak systems more than strong ones. Countries with effective urban planning, resilient infrastructure and functional emergency management systems are far better equipped to cope with heavy rainfall than societies where planning has long been sacrificed on the altar of expediency.

When floods wreak havoc, death is often inevitable. Every year, lives are lost to collapsed buildings, overflowing rivers, electrocution and vehicles swept away by floodwaters. Families lose loved ones, while others are displaced from homes they have spent years building.

Beyond the tragic loss of lives, there is an enormous economic cost that is hardly ever calculated. Businesses are forced to close, with many workers unable to reach their workplaces. Children miss school because parents naturally prioritise their safety. Food items are destroyed, household property is damaged and vehicles are submerged beyond repair. Farmers also suffer significant losses as farmlands are washed away, thereby worsening food insecurity. These disruptions ultimately affect productivity, healthcare delivery and even insurance costs. A single afternoon of flooding can wipe out millions of naira in economic activity and impose financial burdens that linger long after the floodwaters have receded.

The situation is made worse by the nation’s poor emergency response system, a subject I discussed in this space last week. When streets suddenly become flooded, where are the emergency rescue boats? Where are the flood warning systems? How many cities have dedicated flood-response units that can be deployed within minutes? Are emergency telephone numbers functional during storms? Unfortunately, the answers to many of these questions are far from encouraging. Government agencies often appear only after the damage has already been done, conducting assessments, issuing statements and making promises that are quickly forgotten once the waters recede.

Disaster management should not begin after a disaster has occurred. It should start long before the first drops of rain fall. Early warning systems, public education campaigns, emergency shelters and well-equipped rescue teams should all form part of a comprehensive flood management strategy rather than seasonal responses driven by media attention.

Citizens also share responsibility for making the environment safe, whether it rains or not. The indiscriminate dumping of refuse into drains is something that should no longer be heard of in any community in the 21st century. Building illegally is a time bomb waiting to explode. Ignoring evacuation warnings and deliberately blocking waterways are akin to sitting on a keg of gunpowder. While governments have the primary responsibility of providing infrastructure and enforcing regulations, citizens also have a duty to protect public facilities and obey environmental laws.

What do successful cities do differently? They recognise that flooding is not merely an environmental issue but also an urban planning and governance issue. They invest consistently in drainage maintenance, flood forecasting, modern urban planning, strict building regulations and continuous public education. They understand that prevention is always cheaper than emergency response. These cities have demonstrated that effective flood management is neither impossible nor miraculous. It is simply the product of good planning, political will and sustained investment.

Perhaps what Nigeria should be doing in practical terms includes making drainage maintenance a year-round exercise instead of waiting until the rainy season arrives. Governments should protect natural waterways, digitise flood-risk mapping, stop approving buildings on flood plains, invest substantially in modern urban drainage infrastructure, strengthen emergency response capabilities and enforce sanitation and environmental laws consistently. Also important is the need for greater collaboration among federal, state and local governments, since floodwaters do not recognise political boundaries.

Every rainy season, Nigerians act as though the floods have caught everyone by surprise. They have not. We have simply normalised avoidable disasters. Until governments begin to treat drainage, urban planning and flood control as essential public infrastructure rather than seasonal public relations exercises, every dark cloud will continue to trigger fear instead of relief.

Rain should nourish our cities, not paralyse them. It should sustain livelihoods, not destroy them. When every rainfall becomes a national emergency, the problem is no longer the weather—it is governance.
